vignette: Seng was a 72-year-old refugee aid worker who had dedicated his life to helping others in crisis, a calling that had become both his passion and his burden. His life changed dramatically one fateful day when a terrorist attack struck a crowded market in the city where he had been working. The chaos of that day was burned into his memory-he could still see the panicked faces of people running, hear the deafening explosions, and even feel the ground shake beneath him. In the aftermath, Seng found himself grappling with memories that felt surreal, as if they belonged to someone else. The images haunted him, replaying in his mind like a broken record, making it difficult for him to accept that this was part of his reality. The vividness of those memories intensified his feelings of self-blame. Seng often ruminated on the events, questioning whether he could have done something differently to prevent the tragedy. This self-blame spiraled into a profound guilt that colored his interactions with others. He avoided discussing the incident with his wife and friends, fearing it would lead to conflict or disagreement. He was convinced that if he shared his feelings, he would only burden them with his pain, reinforcing his sense of isolation. Driving had become nearly impossible for him; he couldn't bear the thought of being in a car again, as it reminded him of the chaos he had witnessed that day. He felt trapped, oscillating between moments of hypervigilance and the urge to retreat into the confines of his safe zone, which had shrunk to just a handful of familiar places. In his daily life, Seng found himself increasingly jumpy and easily startled by ordinary sounds-a car backfiring or a door slamming would send him into a panic, as if he were back in the market amidst the chaos. This persistent sense of threat kept the memories of the attack fresh in his mind; each time he felt on edge, those haunting images would rush back, as if he needed to keep reviewing them to stay prepared for any potential danger. This constant sense of threat kept the memories of the attack fresh in his mind; the more on edge he felt, the more vivid and intrusive the recollections became, as if he needed to prepare himself for danger by keeping the past alive. These moments of panic would often trigger vivid memories of the attack, pulling him back into the chaos he wished to forget, reinforcing his belief that he was never truly safe. The hyperawareness of his surroundings became a constant state of being; he felt the need to assess every sound and movement, convinced that danger lurked around every corner. Each time he experienced these heightened states of alertness, his memories of the attack would resurface, further entrenching his belief that the world was a perilous place. The weight of these memories loomed over Seng, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that seemed inescapable. In response to the relentless onslaught of painful images, he began to emotionally distance himself from friends and family, believing that by shutting them out, he could protect them from his suffering while also shielding himself from the emotional turmoil that the memories stirred up. The vividness of those memories made him feel that sharing them would only burden his loved ones and bring the chaos back into their lives, reinforcing his need to withdraw further. In response to the relentless onslaught of painful images, Seng began to emotionally distance himself from friends and family, believing that by shutting them out, he could protect them from his suffering while also shielding himself from the emotional turmoil that the memories stirred up. In an effort to escape the painful images that haunted him, he began emotionally distancing himself from friends and family, convincing himself that by staying aloof, he could shield them from his suffering and protect himself from further pain. The more he tried to avoid thinking about the traumatic event, the more intrusive the memories became. In his attempts to evade the painful recollections, Seng often found himself distracted by mundane tasks, hoping that by keeping busy, he could stave off the memories that threatened to overwhelm him. In his attempts to escape the haunting images, Seng found himself engaging in maladaptive strategies, such as avoiding conversations about his work or steering clear of reminders, believing that if he just didn't think about it, the memories would fade. He often replayed the auditory cues in his mind-the screams, the sirens, the explosion-each replay triggering the same visceral fear he felt that day. Each time he felt that undercurrent of danger, memories of the chaos surged back, prompting him to steer conversations away from his work and any reminders of the attack, believing that avoidance was his safest bet. This constant cycle of threat and memory made it impossible for him to feel truly safe. The persistent sense of danger he felt made the memories of that day more vivid and intrusive, as if the threat amplified the images in his mind, pulling them closer to the surface whenever he felt even slightly unsafe. He felt like a prisoner of his own mind, trapped in a labyrinth of thoughts and sensations that left him weary and withdrawn. Yet, despite the toll this had taken on his life, Seng's desire to help others never waned. He continued to work as an aid worker, but he found himself increasingly disengaged, often avoiding conversations that could lead to deeper connections. The emotional distance he maintained was a protective barrier, but one that left him feeling profoundly lonely. His relationships suffered as he withdrew, unable to share the burden of his trauma with those closest to him. After months of battling these overwhelming feelings and symptoms, Seng finally reached a breaking point. The weight of his unresolved trauma, coupled with the isolation he felt from his loved ones, compelled him to seek help. He hoped to find a way to reclaim his sense of safety and connection, fearful that his memories would continue to dictate his life if he did not confront them. As he sat in the waiting room, he felt a flicker of hope, mingled with trepidation-could he really begin to heal from this pain? He learned that during those moments of heightened anxiety, the memories would flood back with even more intensity, making him feel as though he had no choice but to avoid situations that reminded him of that day.
